newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine pension funds opt for more streamlining.
newsitem.headline: Argentine pension funds opt for more streamlining.

text.p: Argentina's latest private pension fund buyout underlines the streamlining of the industry which should speed up the funds' growth and lead to greater efficiency, analysts say.
"We like it, it's good news and it's not going to stop," said Peter Schubert, an analyst at Mexican brokerage Interacciones.

Pension fund Origenes AFJP said last week it will buy the shares of fund manager's Activa-Anticipar for around $100 million. When the deal is approved in a couple of months Origenes will become the largest Argentine private pension fund with $600 million under management and 930,000 members.
Origenes is jointly owned by Banco de la Provincia de Buenos Aires and Spain's Banco Santander.
"There is an important and natural tendency of concentration" in the industry, said Hugo Dias Lourenco, chief economist at private consultancy C&E Consultores.
So far, the pension fund industry manages $4.0 billion and has 5.3 million members. It is projected to manage $20 billion by 2000.
When the private pension fund industry was introduced in July 1994 there were 26 funds and after this latest merger 21 remain.
Schubert said, "There are too many players in a market of this size." He thinks eventually there will only be 15 funds left.

Ricardo Guitart, general manager of pension fund Siembra AFJP, agrees. "There is an undeniable reality that many funds still have results in the red but this industry requires, due to its high structural costs, significantly large economies of scale," he said.

And larger institutions will offer members more choice in products. As Rodolfo Frigeri, President of Banco de la Provincia de Buenos Aires, said: "The fund's size will give it a superior range of services that will allow it to be more profitable in the market."

The economies of scale brought about by mergers such as the one announced this week will make the industry leaner, ultimately benefiting local capital markets and potentially accelerating sought-after changes in the way the funds can invest.

The funds can still only invest 2.5 percent in a single stock, although that was recently raised from 1.5 percent. Of the total funds managed, 35 percent may be invested in quoted stocks, with a limit of 14 percent in stocks of privatized companies. The rest of the funds are mainly invested in bonds.
Streamlining of the industry should "speed up the process of diversification," said Schubert.
With the government still planning to privatize a number of large state enterprises, a system allowing the funds bigger participation in privatized firms would be especially welcome, say analysts.

Argentine capital market players hope the private pension fund industry can eventually become a powerful force, helping finance the development of industry and allowing the government to gradually replace its overseas debt with local bonds, all of which should help modernize the economy further.
Many observers cautiously predict the funds could in time play the same role as they have done in the development of the economy in neighboring Chile.
